title: Egress smoothing and 'drip' chunking: exploratory benchmark notes
content:
Summary:

This note records an exploratory benchmark investigating a lightweight egress-smoothing heuristic we prototyped ("drip" chunking) to reduce head-of-line and tail amplification caused by asynchronous client write patterns + proxy buffering. Goal: quantify p95/p99 tail impacts, CPU cost on edge proxies, and interactions with KV cache warmup under mixed client write behaviours.

Why we care: we repeatedly see applications (chat widgets, mobile SDKs) that write token-by-token or in micro-bursts. When those clients sit behind an L7 proxy that flushes or multiplexes differently than the downstream connection expects, we get amplified tails (p99 -> 2x-4x) even when p50 is fine. Current mitigations (client-side coalesce, proxy-level fixed-window buffering) are brittle across heterogeneous clients.

Hypotheses tested:
- H1: short, configurable egress-smoothing (tiny coalesce window + max-chunk-size) reduces p99 by absorbing micro-bursts without materially increasing p50.
- H2: egress-smoothing reduces proxy CPU spikes caused by frequent syscalls from many tiny writes.
- H3: When KV cache is cold, smoothing can slightly hurt throughput because it holds initial bytes; effect is small for window <= 8ms.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Clients:
  * flush-each-token (worst-case, mobile SDK naive)
  * batched-50ms (buffering in app)
  * steady-200-token (large single write)
- Proxy modes:
  * baseline (no coalesce, immediate write)
  * fixed-packet-coalesce (our previous 8KB watermark approach)
  * drip-chunking (coalesce-window=6ms, max-coalesce-bytes=4KB, prefer-first-byte-immediate=true)
- Transport: HTTP/2 (h2 over TLS) and gRPC (h2 with multiplexing)
- Workload: 100 concurrent connections from 200 clients, inference backend producing ~120 tokens per request at avg generation rate 60 tokens/s.
- Duration: 15m runs, 3 repeats each config.

Hardware/software baseline:
- Edge proxy: 4x c6i.4xlarge (4vCPU each) behind TLS offload lb (same lab config used for previous proxy work).
- Inference nodes: 2x g-type (same as p99-target cluster), KV cache warmup toggled via synthetic pre-seed.
- Serving runtime: v0.62.1 (baseline), experimental proxy patch applied locally.

Metrics collected:
- Latency per request (p50/p90/p95/p99), measured at client side and at proxy egress.
- CPU% and syscall rate on proxy workers.
- Egress packetization pattern: write sizes histogram, TLS record sizes, http2 DATA frame sizes.
- Throughput (requests/s), error rate, and connection churn.

Key results (aggregated across repeats):
- Baseline (flush-each-token): p50=42ms, p95=220ms, p99=560ms; proxy CPU avg=45%, syscall rate high (~5800 syscalls/s)
- Fixed-packet-coalesce: p50=45ms, p95=190ms, p99=310ms; proxy CPU avg=36%, syscall rate reduced (~3200 syscalls/s)
- Drip-chunking (6ms/4KB): p50=47ms, p95=135ms, p99=180ms; proxy CPU avg=30%, syscall rate low (~1600 syscalls/s)
- For batched-50ms client, differences are small across modes (p99 within ±10%), but drip still reduced CPU by ~10%.

Observations and interpretation:
- Drip-chunking gives the best tail reduction for pathological clients (flush-each-token), with p99 improvement ~3x vs baseline. The small p50 increase (~5ms) is acceptable for most interactive workloads.
- The mechanism reduces syscall frequency significantly by combining many tiny writes into fewer TLS records. TLS record coalescing reduces kernel->user transitions and measurable CPU time on proxy workers.
- The fixed-packet-coalesce approach (watermark-based) helps but is brittle: it occasionally introduces bigger stalls when many clients hit the watermark at the same time, producing synchronized bursts seen in proxy egress traces.
- Drip-chunking avoids synchronized batching by using short time-based window + max-bytes; this smooths flow without synchronizing across clients.
- When KV cache was intentionally cold before runs, drip-chunking increased the time-to-first-byte by ~8-12ms for some requests. But p99 remained overall lower than baseline because it prevented subsequent amplify effects.

Microtraces (representative):
- Baseline flush-each-token: sequence of 120 small writes (40-80 bytes) -> 120 TLS records -> many small h2 DATA frames -> proxy CPU spikes and queueing, tail increases.
- Drip: groupings of writes resulted in ~18 TLS records (avg 2.7KB) for same response, much flatter CPU profile.

Tradeoffs and gotchas:
- If coalesce window is too long (>12ms) user-perceivable latency increases. Default window should be <= 8ms for interactive features.
- Max-coalesce-bytes must be tuned per-model response sizes; too small and syscall reduction benefit is lost; too large and we create head delays.
- TLS offload and upstream multiplexers interact: if TLS is offloaded at LB, proxy must consider post-offload socket semantics; some metrics above assume TLS on-proxy.

Actionable recommendations:
1) Ship a conservative drip-chunking heuristic in the edge proxy behind a feature flag: default coalesce-window=6ms, max-bytes=4KB, first-byte-pass-through enabled.
2) Expose client-side SDK knob (suggested default 8ms coalesce) and recommend to PLG SDKs to adopt it; SDK-level smoothing is still best place when available.
3) Add egress-smoothing telemetry: write_size_hist, tls_record_size_hist, coalesce_events_count per connection to make regressions visible in Console.
4) For Dedicated offering, document the interaction with TLS-offload setups and provide a deployment checklist for owners.

Next experiments / TODOs:
- Expand matrix to QUIC/HTTP3: early prototyping suggests similar benefits, but we need dedicated runs. (JIRA:INFR-4906)
- Re-run with mixed tenant workloads to check fairness when a few noisy tenants cause coalescing pressure.
- Validate with TLS-offload (LB terminates TLS) to measure effect when coalescing happens after offload.
- Evaluate interaction with server push and function-calling payloads (larger structured output).
- Add small A/B in production on low-traffic region for 24h to verify non-lab artifacts (followup: INFR-4821-AB).

Open questions / discussion points:
- Should coalescing be per-connection or per-tenant? Per-connection is simpler but tenant-level smoothing could coordinate better for multi-connection apps.
- Does coalescing change replay behavior or monitoring expectations for some customers that rely on per-token metrics? Need buy-in from observability team.
- How to present smoothing in Console: as an optimization (recommended) or as an escape hatch for noisy clients?

Experiment artifacts and scripts:
- runner: /bench/egress/drip-runner.sh (local lab), parameters: --window-ms --max-bytes --clients --duration
- trace collector: /bench/egress/collect-traces.py -> outputs per-run p50/p95/p99 and tls-record histograms
- quick plot: /bench/egress/plotting/egress_coalesce_2026.ipynb

Notes to self:
- Share initial A/B plan with Solutions Eng and CS before rolling default on hosted. Some customers will prefer opt-out.
- Coordinate with observability to add coalesce metrics to service spans (low effort: increment counter on coalesce event).

References and related work in Drive:
- Related proxy backpressure notes (see JIRA ref in linked artifacts)
- Prior experiments that inspired drip approach: adaptive-proxy-pacing-windowing-latency-sweep-aug-2026 (internal)

End of note.

(Informal, rough; will tidy once we pick next experiment to run.)
